Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 93, verses 1–4:

﴿By the morning brightness﴾. In the case of "ad-Duha" (the forenoon) it is mentioned in "ash-Shams wa-duhaha" (By the sun and its brightness). ﴿And by the night when it covers (or grows still)﴾. On the meaning of "idha saja" there are four opinions: when it approaches (aqbala), when it withdraws (adbara), when it becomes dark (adhlama), and when it becomes still (sakana), i.e., settles and becomes level, or when people and sounds become still in it. From the same root comes the expression "layla sajiya" (a still night), meaning a night when the wind is calm, and "tarf saj" (a steady gaze), or one that is still and does not move about. This last is closer in derivation (ishtiqaq), and it is the choice of Ibn 'Atiyya. ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He come to hate you﴾. "Wada'aka" is read with the doubled dal, from the verb "wada'" (to bid farewell/to forsake), and it has been recited with the dal unstressed, meaning: "has not left you." The word "wada'" is used as an intensified form of "tark" (leaving). ﴿Nor has He come to hate you (qala)﴾, i.e., He has not come to hate you. The object pronoun is omitted from "qala," "awa," "hada," and "aghna," for brevity, since the meaning is clear and it accords with the endings of the verses. The occasion of revelation was that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was delayed in receiving revelation, so the Quraysh said: "Muhammad's Lord has forsaken him and come to hate him." So the verse was revealed as a refutation of them. It is also said that the Prophet (peace be upon him) was struck by a stone on his finger, which bled, and he remained for two or three nights unable to stand. A woman said: "I see that Muhammad's devil has only left him." So the verse was revealed. ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first (life)﴾, i.e., the Abode of the Hereafter is better for you than this world. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It may be that by 'the Hereafter' is meant his condition after the revelation of this surah, and by 'the first' his condition at the time of its revelation. But this is far-fetched, and the first view is more apparent and better known."

﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied.﴾ It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When this was revealed, I would not be content if a single one of my community remained in the Fire." Some of them said: "This is the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an." Ibn ʿAbbas said: his satisfaction is that Allah promised him a thousand palaces in Paradise, with what he needs of blessings and servants. It was also said: his satisfaction in this world is the conquest of Makkah and other things. The correct view is that it is a promise encompassing everything Allah gives him in the Hereafter, and everything He gave him in this world of victory, conquests, the multiplication of Muslims, and other things.

﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ Allah enumerates His blessings upon him in the past of his life, so that he may measure the future by them, his heart may be at ease, and his hope may be strengthened. The verb "wajada" in these places takes two objects and is in the sense of "ʿalima" (to know). The meaning is: "Were you not an orphan, and He sheltered you?" This is because his father, peace be upon him, died while he was in his mother's womb, then his mother died when he was five years old, and it was also said eight. His grandfather ʿAbd al-Muttalib then took charge of him, and when he died, leaving him at the age of twelve, his uncle Abu Talib took charge of him. It was said to Jaʿfar al-Sadiq: "Why did Allah make the Prophet ﷺ an orphan?" He said: "So that no right of any created being would be upon him."

﴿And He found you lost and guided you.﴾ There are six opinions regarding this. The first: He found you ignorant of the Shariʿah (sharīʿah, the sacred law), and He guided you to it. Here "ḍalāl" (going astray) means being perplexed in matters of religion until the truth came to him from Allah. It is like His saying: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. This is the most apparent view, and it is what Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and others chose. Its meaning is that he did not know the details of the Shariʿah and its branches until Allah sent him, but he never disbelieved in Allah nor associated anything with Him, because he was protected from that before and after prophethood. The second: He found you among a misguided people, so you were like one of them, though you did not worship what they worshipped; this is close to the first. The third: He found you lost concerning emigration (hijrah) and guided you to it; this is weak, because the surah was revealed before the Hijrah. The fourth: He found you bearing the message without knowing it, and He guided people to you and guided you through them; this is far from the intended meaning. The fifth: that it is from losing the way: he ﷺ got lost in some quarter of Makkah while he was young, and Allah returned him to his grandfather. It was also said: he got lost from his foster mother Halimah, and Allah returned him to her. It was also said: he got lost on the road to Syria when he went out there with Abu Talib. The sixth: that it means straying in the sense of love, i.e., He found you loving Allah and guided you to Him. From this is the saying of Joseph's brothers to their father: ﴿By Allah, you are surely in your old error﴾ [Yusuf: 95], meaning your love for Yusuf. Our shaykh, al-Ustadh Abu Jaʿfar Ibn al-Zubayr, used to say this.

﴿And He found you poor and made you self-sufficient.﴾ The ʿāʾil is the poor person; it is said: "ʿāla al-rajul" (the man became poor), so he is ʿāʾil when he is in need; and "aʿāla," so he is muʿīl, when his dependents become many. This poverty and wealth concern wealth, and his ﷺ self-sufficiency is that Allah gave him sufficiency (al-kafāf, what is enough). It was also said: it is his contentment with what Allah gave him. It was also said: the meaning is: He found you in need of Him, so He made you self-sufficient through Him.

﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress.﴾ That is, do not overpower him regarding his wealth and his right because of his weakness, or do not oppress him by preventing his interests; the forms of oppression are many, and the prohibition encompasses all of them.

﴿And as for the one who asks, do not repel.﴾ Nahr is rebuffing and rebuking. The prohibition against it is a command to speak kindly and to supplicate for the one who asks, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord, then speak to them gently﴾ [al-Isra': 28]. The "one who asks" may mean one who asks for food and wealth, and this is the most apparent view; and one who asks about knowledge and religion. In His saying "taqhar" and "tanhar" there is the obligation of a rhyme that does not otherwise require the letter ha before ra.

The third: He found you lost concerning emigration (hijrah) and guided you to it; this is weak, because the surah was revealed before the Hijrah.
